A mural is a large work of art — almost always a painting or image — created directly on a wall, ceiling, or other large, fixed surface. Unlike a regular painting on canvas that can be taken down and moved, a mural is made onto the surface itself, making it a permanent part of the space it belongs to.

That is the single most important thing to understand: a mural lives on the structure, not just in it.

Murals are almost always big — often covering an entire wall or ceiling from edge to edge. This large scale is intentional. Murals are meant to be seen from a distance, to fill a space dramatically, and to make a strong visual impact. A small doodle on a wall is not a mural; a mural commands attention.

Outdoors (exterior murals): Painted on the outside walls of buildings — factories, apartment blocks, schools, bridges, and tunnels. Common in cities, where they transform plain concrete walls into something vibrant.

Indoors (interior murals): Found on the walls and ceilings inside buildings — churches, government buildings, museums, hospitals, restaurants, and even homes. One of the most famous murals in the world is the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, painted by Michelangelo — a breathtaking interior mural covering over 500 square metres of ceiling.

The most common method is paint, applied directly to the wall with brushes, rollers, or spray cans. But murals can also be created using:

  • Fresco — an ancient technique where paint is applied to wet plaster. As the plaster dries, the paint becomes chemically locked into the wall permanently. The Sistine Chapel is a fresco mural.
  • Mosaic — small pieces of coloured glass, stone, or tile arranged on a wall to form an image.
  • Spray paint — especially common in street art. Many large-scale spray-painted images on city walls are murals.
  • Ceramic tiles — hand-painted or printed tiles installed on a wall surface.

What makes something a mural is where it is (on a fixed wall or surface), not how it was made.

Decoration and beauty: The most basic purpose — to make a dull, plain space more alive and visually interesting.

Storytelling and history: Murals have been used for thousands of years to tell stories. Ancient cave paintings are the earliest examples. Later, civilisations painted murals in temples and palaces to record historical events, mythological stories, and the achievements of rulers.

Community and cultural identity: A mural can express what a community values, who its heroes are, or what it has endured. Cities around the world have murals honouring local figures, celebrating heritage, or commemorating loss.

Political and social messages: Because of their large size and public visibility, murals are a powerful tool for protest, advocacy, and social commentary. A mural can speak a message to thousands of people who simply walk past it every day.

Religious and spiritual purposes: Churches, temples, and mosques across many cultures feature murals depicting religious figures, stories, and sacred themes.
Mural vs. things that seem similar

A painting on canvas: A regular painting is portable — it can be rolled up, moved, sold, or stored. A mural cannot be moved without destroying it. This is the sharpest distinction.

Graffiti: Graffiti is writing or drawing on a wall, typically done without permission. A mural can look like graffiti (especially spray-painted street art), but murals are generally authorised — the artist was given permission or was paid (commissioned) to create the work. The line can blur: a large, detailed, spray-painted image is often called a mural regardless of whether it had permission, especially if it shows clear artistic intent and craftsmanship.

A fresco: A fresco is a type of mural — specifically one made by painting on wet plaster. All frescoes are murals, but not all murals are frescoes.

A mosaic: A mosaic can be a mural when it is wall-mounted and forms a large image. When people picture a mural, they usually imagine something painted, but the word extends to mosaics on walls too.

A mural vs. a "wall painting": These two phrases mean the same thing. "Mural" is simply the more formal and widely used term.

• "The city commissioned an artist to paint a mural on the side of the railway station."
  • "The school's corridor had a mural showing children from different parts of India."
  • "Tourists gathered to photograph the mural that stretched across the entire five-storey building."
  • "The mural inside the old church depicted scenes from the life of a saint."
  • "After the floods, the community created a mural to remember those they had lost."
  • "The mural was so detailed that it looked almost like a photograph from a distance."
A mural is a large artwork — typically a painting — made directly on a wall or ceiling, permanent, and designed to be seen by many people in the space it occupies.
